meta.title: Yuelong (John) Guo — Science, AI Education & Community
meta.description: Yuelong (John) Guo is a scientist working across computational pathology, proteomic biomarker discovery, and large-scale human genomics, and a volunteer AI educator and community leader in North Carolina.

profile.name: Yuelong (John) Guo
profile.role: Two questions drive everything I do: what is the mechanism underneath, and how do I put that understanding into someone else's hands?
profile.introduction: I use computation and AI to find the mechanism behind a biomarker, an image, or a genome — and I teach the same tools to students, so they can open the black box instead of admiring it.

research.title: Histology imaging & molecular subtyping
research.summary: Joining histology imaging with molecular subtyping: using routine stained slides to assign cancer patients to subtypes ordinarily defined by expression profiling. The premise is that the transcriptional programs separating those subtypes leave signatures in tissue architecture and nuclear morphology, so a slide already cut for diagnosis can carry information otherwise bought with a separate molecular assay. The difficulty is generalization — a subtype label belongs to the patient while morphology varies from field to field across a whole slide, and stain and scanner variation between sites is easily mistaken for biological signal.

research.title: Blood systems genomics
research.summary: The largest thread in the record: donor genetics, red blood cell storage biology, and hemolysis across a multi-ancestry cohort of more than 13,000 blood donors.

research.title: Statistical genetics & GWAS

research.title: Sickle cell disease cohorts
research.summary: Clinical and genetic ancestry profiling in a large multi-centre Brazilian sickle cell disease cohort, and the genetic predictors of its complications.

research.title: Oncology pharmacogenomics
research.summary: Pediatric Preclinical Testing Consortium evaluations of targeted agents in childhood leukemia and solid tumours, plus immunogenomic profiling of response to checkpoint inhibitors and high-dose IL-2.

research.title: Genetical genomics

about.headline: Find the mechanism. Hand it to someone else.
paragraphs: I have spent my career asking the same question of very different systems: what is the mechanism underneath? Plant and nematode genomes gave way to human population genetics, transfusion medicine to neurodegeneration — but the method never changed. Define the measurement carefully, respect what the data can and cannot support, and leave behind an analysis someone else can reproduce.

AI changed the pace of that work rather than its nature. It lets me search a proteome or a stack of images for structure I would never have found by hand, and it collapses the distance between having an idea and testing it. What it does not do is explain itself — which is exactly why I teach it the way I do.

In the classroom I would rather a student understand one algorithm from the inside than run ten of them as black boxes. My courses open at linear regression and build upward, because the intuition transfers even as the tools keep changing. The aim is always the same: give someone enough understanding to go and build the thing they were already imagining.
The volunteer work comes from the same place. A community, like a model, only works when enough people are willing to look under the hood and explain what they find.
